grammar.title: Present Perfect Continuous
grammar.explanation:
We use the **present perfect continuous** for actions that started in the past and are still happening now. The form is **have/has been + verb-ing**. I **have been cooking** since noon — the meat is finally tender.

Use **since** for a start point and **for** for a length of time. She **has been sewing** **since** eight this morning. The **tailor** **has been working** on my **outfit** **for** two hours.

It also explains a present result. He **has been staring** at that **screen** **for** three hours — his eyes hurt. The action is finished, but we can see the result now.

They **have been selling** **vintage** clothes **since** 2019. Their **trendy** jackets are the best sellers, and a silk **accessory** is their newest product.

Common mistake: do NOT use the continuous form with state verbs like **know**, **like**, or **belong**. Say I **have known** him for years — never I **have been knowing** him. Also check the **data** in your sentence: subject + **have/has** must agree.
examples: *I have been cooking* since noon — the chicken is finally tender. (the action is still happening)
*She has been working* as a tailor for ten years. (for + a long time span)
*They have been waiting* for their stopover flight since six. (still waiting now)
*He has been checking* the data all morning. (recent action with a result now)
*We have been listening* to the new speaker for an hour. (a continuous activity)
*You have been wearing* that vintage outfit since Monday! (still true now)

practice.q: Complete: I ___ (cook) since noon — the meat is tender now.
practice.a: have been cooking. Say: I have been cooking since noon.

practice.q: Complete: She ___ (work) as a tailor for ten years.
practice.a: has been working. Say: She has been working as a tailor for ten years.

practice.q: Choose: They ___ (wait / have been waiting) for their stopover since six.
practice.a: have been waiting. Say: They have been waiting for their stopover since six.

practice.q: Fix the mistake: I have been knowing him for years.
practice.a: I have known him for years. State verbs like know never take the continuous form.
